Dear Pinecrest Insights Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Analyst (New Grad, 2027) position. I'm a senior at Brookfield University studying Computer Science with a minor in Data Science, and I'll graduate in May 2027. Pinecrest's focus on helping education, healthcare, and nonprofit organizations understand the people they serve is the kind of work I've been moving toward through my internship and my research.

Last summer I was a Data Analyst Intern at Brightpath Learning, an ed-tech company. I built a Tableau dashboard that the product team used to track weekly active students, lessons completed, and learning streaks, and I wrote the SQL behind it. While building the tables I found that sessions were being double-counted when students put the app in the background. I fixed this by defining a session as activity with gaps under 30 minutes, using window functions over event timestamps. The team found the streak breakdown by grade level especially useful. That project showed me that a dashboard is only useful if people can trust the numbers under it.

Since October 2025 I've been an undergraduate research assistant in Brookfield's Social Computing Lab. I work on an interview study, led by a PhD student, about how teens aged 15 to 17 use online communities for mental-health support. I sent recruitment messages and ran the eligibility screener. I also transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews, replacing names, schools, and community names with placeholders. Later I coded 6 transcripts with the team's codebook and took part in inter-rater reliability checks, reaching a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 with my mentor after one round of reconciliation. This work taught me to handle sensitive youth data carefully and to code open-ended responses consistently. I'd like to bring both skills to Pinecrest's survey work and to the client interviews I'd help run with senior researchers.

In a Machine Learning course project, my team of three fine-tuned a transformer to classify sentiment in Reddit support posts. It reached a macro-F1 of 0.81, compared with 0.72 for a TF-IDF baseline. I led the error analysis and found that the model often labeled sarcastic or darkly humorous posts as negative. That's a good example of why I like pairing quantitative results with a close reading of what people actually wrote.

I'd be glad to grow through Pinecrest's mentorship program and its rotations across client domains. Thank you for your consideration. I'd welcome the chance to talk.

Sincerely,
Avery Santos

**Statement of Interest: PhD in Human-Computer Interaction, Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

For the past year I've been an undergraduate research assistant in the Social Computing Lab at Brookfield University. My role has been small. The lab is running an interview study, led by a PhD student, about how teens use online communities for mental-health support. I've helped with the behind-the-scenes parts: sending recruitment messages, transcribing and de-identifying interviews, and coding some of the transcripts with the team's codebook. I didn't design the study or run the interviews. But spending that many hours with people's own words changed how I think about the technology they use.

One interview has stayed with me. A teen described an online community that was the one place they felt they could say they were having a bad day. Then the moderators added a bot that automatically deleted posts with certain words, and some of their posts just disappeared. [Optional, if J. Kim approves: They called it "being shushed by a robot."] I understand why the moderators did it, since they were probably trying to keep people safe. Still, I keep wondering who tools like that are really for, and what they miss about the people they're supposed to protect.

I'd run into a smaller version of this before. In a machine learning class, my team built a model to classify the sentiment of posts in a mental-health support forum. I did the error analysis, and it was the only part of the project I really enjoyed. The model kept labeling sarcastic or darkly funny posts as negative. To the model they looked the same as distress. To the people writing them, they were often a way of coping. At the time I saw it as an interesting mistake. After the interview, I started seeing it as the same problem with real consequences.

I don't have a research question worked out yet, and I don't want to pretend I do. The closest I can get is this: when automated systems decide what vulnerable people mean, what do they get wrong, and could those systems be designed with those people in mind? I don't yet know how to study that well, or whether I'd approach it through interviews, building something, or both. Learning how to do that is a big part of why I want a PhD.

At Khoury, I'm interested in Prof. Tianshi Li's lab, which looks at how people oversee AI systems that act on their behalf and how online communities respond to censorship. [A sentence in your own words after reading one paper.] I'm also interested in [second faculty member], whose work on [online communities or moderation] [connection].

I'm not sure yet exactly what kind of researcher I'll be. I do know I want to keep working on this question. The parts of my work that felt most meaningful were the slow ones, like reading closely, noticing what didn't fit, and asking why. I'd like to spend the next several years learning to do that properly.
